Populations of the African giant threadfin Polydactylus quadrifilis inhabiting the coastal waters of the Gulf of Guinea exhibit remarkable maximum sizes, with individuals attaining a total length of up to 200 centimeters [Li = up to 200 centimeters]. This large ultimate body length positions the species as one of the largest polynemids in the region, with body proportions that likely confer advantages in pursuing swift, schooling prey across open sandy substrates. Field surveys employing gillnets and longlines indicate that such asymptotic dimensions are reached only after many years of sustained growth, during which the fish allocate resources primarily to structural development and the accumulation of somatic tissue. The substantial body size also influences the species’ conspicuous reproductive ecology, as larger females typically produce more numerous batches of pelagic eggs, contributing to a broad and possibly spatially structured spawning stock. Understanding the maximum attainable length is therefore critical for stock assessment models and for setting appropriate minimum size limits to ensure that individuals have the opportunity to reproduce before encountering fishing mortality. Length-frequency distributions from multiple independent studies consistently yield an upper asymptote near this 200-centimeter mark, confirming its utility as a benchmark for life-history comparisons across the genus.

Reproductive development in Polydactylus quadrifilis is characterized by a total length at puberty of 82.5 centimeters [Lp = 82.5 centimeters], indicating that sexual maturity is attained well before the species reaches its ultimate length. This metric is derived from histological examinations of gonadal tissue across a broad size gradient, revealing that the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermatogenesis in males consistently occurs near this fork-length benchmark. The transition from an energetically demanding juvenile growth phase to one that balances further increases in body size with the initiation of gamete production represents a key life-history trade-off. At this length, the fish have typically spent a substantial portion of their early life accumulating sufficient energy reserves to support the high metabolic demands of reproductive events. The 82.5-centimeter mark is therefore a vital parameter for fisheries management, as it defines the size threshold below which individuals should be protected to maintain the spawning potential of the population. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the onset of maturity at roughly two-fifths of the asymptotic length is a common pattern amongst large-bodied polynemids.

The initial ontogenetic stages of Polydactylus quadrifilis begin with a fertilized ovum that is approximately 0.775 millimeters in diameter, a typical size for pelagic eggs within the family Polynemidae, from which the wet weight at birth is calculated to be 0.00024 grams [Wwb = 0.00024 grams]. This minuscule yolk-laden egg undergoes rapid cleavage and embryonic development shortly after broadcast spawning in the water column, where the transparent chorion allows direct observation of the developing embryo. Following a brief incubation period, chorion rupture releases a yolk-sac larva that remains entirely reliant on its endogenous yolk reserves for several days. The extraordinarily low neonatal mass reflects the high fecundity typical of many marine teleosts, enabling the production of millions of offspring over a single spawning season despite the tiny size of each individual larva. The larval phase is characterized by a dramatic increase in mortality, with only a minuscule fraction surviving through the first exogenous feeding stage to eventually recruit into the juvenile population. This initial mass sets the energetic baseline from which all subsequent growth trajectories emerge.

Under controlled laboratory conditions simulating the thermal regime of the eastern Atlantic, the maximum lifespan of African giant threadfin has been estimated at 8030 days [am = 8030 days] at 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This longevity estimate, derived from mark-recapture studies and validated by otolith microchemistry from the largest individuals sampled, positions the species as a relatively long-lived member of the polynemid assemblage. The extended lifespan allows for multiple reproductive seasons, which is expected given the high energetic investment per spawning event and the reliance on episodic, environmentally driven recruitment windows. At this stable temperature, metabolic processes appear to proceed at a rate that does not accelerate senescence unduly, consistent with the metabolic theory of ecology. This lifespan, equivalent to approximately 22 years of sustained growth and reproductive activity, has direct implications for sustainable harvest levels, as populations with such protracted generation times are inherently more vulnerable to overexploitation. The fidelity of the age estimate is reinforced by consistent counts of annual increments in sagittal otoliths from specimens spanning the full size range.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of female Polydactylus quadrifilis is 5.5% [GSI = 5.5%] at 26 °C [T = 26 °C] during the peak of the spawning season. This relatively moderate allocation, measured against the backdrop of the species’ ultimate weight of 85,000 grams [Wwi = 85,000 grams], suggests an iteroparous strategy in which females partition their energetic resources across multiple annual spawning bouts rather than investing heavily in a single, massive reproductive event. The thermal regime of 26 °C appears to be optimal for these physiological processes, falling within the typical sea-surface temperatures of the species’ equatorial range. Such life-history parameters are essential inputs for demographic models used in assessing the sustainability of artisanal and industrial fisheries targeting this species.
